title: Extraction of high-quality RNA from mouse pancreatic tumors
author: Chougoni, Grossman
materials: Step 3: Purification and Isolation of RNA3.1.After mixing with ethanol, transfer the mixture to the QIAGEN RNeasy mini spin column and centrifuge at 9600 rcf for 30 s.3.2.Wash the column using 350 µl RW1 wash buffer from the RNeasy mini extraction kit.3.3.Add 40 µl of freshly prepared DNase I solution (Thermo Fisher) and incubate the column for 15 min at RT, after which, wash the column with RW1 wash buffer for the second time and centrifuge at 9600 rcf for 30 s. This eliminates DNA contamination of the extracted RNA.3.4.Discard the flow through, and wash the column with 500 µl RPE buffer supplied in the kit two times at 9600 rcf for 30 s.3.5.Finally, spin the column at 16,000 rcf for 2 min to remove any remaining RPE buffer from column. Make sure you remove the RPE buffer completely for better results.3.6.Add 30–40 µl of RNase free water to the column and incubate the column for 1 min at room temperature.3.7.Centrifuge at 9600 rcf for 30 s to collect the pure RNA.3.8.Tip: Avoid including tissue pieces in the solution that might result in blocking of the column and reduce column efficiency.3.9.Tip: As the binding affinity of the RNase easy spin columns is limited, we recommend dividing the total extract into equal volumes and using multiple columns to avoid clogging of the columns and combine the eluates after isolation to restore sufficient volume.3.10.Tip: Avoid repeated elution, as most of the RNA obtained by repeated elution is not high enough quality for sequencing purposes.

Step 4: Quantification of RNA4.1.The concentration of RNA is measured using a Nanodrop (Thermo Scientific, USA) by loading 2 µl of the sample.4.2.The concentration and the absorbance ratio A260/A280 value obtained in the Nanodrop gives an estimate of concentration and any protein contamination.4.3.However, 260/280 value is not a determinant of intact RNA, so make sure you have sufficient RNA for the quality check and sequencing steps.

steps.title: Isolate and Freeze Tumor Tissue
steps.instruction: Inject four‑month‑old NSG mice orthotopically in the pancreatic tail with 8 × 10⁵ PDAC cells; allow tumors to grow for three weeks. Decontaminate the workspace and all surgical tools with 70 % ethanol and RNase Zap wipes. Anesthetize mice with isoflurane, euthanize by cervical dislocation, and fix them ventral side up on a dissecting table. Sterilize the abdomen with 70 % ethanol, make a longitudinal genital incision, move the bowels leftward, incise the common bile duct, and quickly isolate the pancreas using scissors and forceps (sterile conditions not required for RNA extraction). If only part of the tumor is needed, cut the tumor while it is soaked in RNA stabilizing agent in a petri dish on ice, transfer the piece to a vial or Eppendorf tube, drop it into liquid nitrogen to flash‑freeze, and store at –80 °C until extraction. Be as quick as possible and keep everything cold. Mince the tumor or pancreas into small pieces while soaked in RNA stabilizing agent to improve reagent penetration and RNA integrity. For long‑term storage, tissues may be soaked in RNA stabilizing agent before extraction and stored according to the manufacturer’s specifications; however, snap‑freezing in liquid nitrogen and storing at –80 °C gives the best results for next‑day extraction.

steps.title: Prepare Equipment and Reagents
steps.instruction: Clean the mortar and pestle with RNaseZap wipes. Place the pestle in the mortar and add liquid nitrogen to chill both. Keep TRIzol solution on ice or use it immediately after removal from the refrigerator.

steps.title: Grind Tissue and Add TRIzol
steps.instruction: Tare a weighing boat on a balance, transfer the flash‑frozen pancreas/tumor tissue from its vial into the boat, record the weight, and quickly move the tissue to the pre‑cooled mortar. Powder the tissue with liquid nitrogen, keeping everything frozen; do not allow the tissue to thaw. After the liquid nitrogen evaporates, add TRIzol in 500 µl aliquots at a ratio of 500 µl per 50 mg tissue (up to 1 ml per 100 mg for optimal yield). Triturate the mixture in a chemical hood until the lysate is fully liquefied.

steps.title: Incubate and Perform Phase Separation
steps.instruction: Transfer the TRIzol lysate to a DNase/RNase‑free Eppendorf tube and incubate for 5 min at room temperature (the lysate may solidify briefly and then liquefy with continued trituration). Add 200 µl chloroform per 1 ml of TRIzol lysate, shake vigorously for 15 s, and incubate for 2–3 min at room temperature. Centrifuge the tube in a pre‑cooled centrifuge (4 °C) at 11 600 rcf for 15 min.

steps.title: Collect Aqueous Phase and Precipitate
steps.instruction: After centrifugation, carefully transfer the upper clear aqueous phase to a fresh Eppendorf tube without disturbing the lower organic layer. Add 0.5 × volume of 100 % ethanol to the aqueous phase to precipitate nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).

steps.title: Spin Column Purification
steps.instruction: Load the ethanol‑mixed lysate onto a QIAGEN RNeasy Mini spin column and centrifuge at 9 600 rcf for 30 s. Wash the column with 350 µl RW1 buffer. Add 40 µl freshly prepared DNase I (Thermo Fisher) directly onto the membrane, incubate the column for 15 min at room temperature, then wash again with 350 µl RW1 and centrifuge at 9 600 rcf for 30 s. Discard the flow‑through and wash the column twice with 500 µl RPE buffer, each wash followed by centrifugation at 9 600 rcf for 30 s. Spin the column at 16 000 rcf for 2 min to remove residual RPE; ensure the buffer is completely removed. Add 30–40 µl RNase‑free water to the membrane, incubate for 1 min at room temperature, and centrifuge at 9 600 rcf for 30 s to elute pure RNA. Avoid introducing tissue fragments that could clog the column. If the total extract volume exceeds the column capacity, divide the lysate among multiple columns, elute separately, and combine the eluates. Do not perform repeated elutions, as they reduce RNA quality for sequencing.

steps.title: Quantify RNA Concentration
steps.instruction: Measure RNA concentration with a Nanodrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA) by loading 2 µl of the eluate. Record the concentration and the A260/A280 absorbance ratio to assess protein contamination; note that the ratio does not indicate RNA integrity.

steps.title: Assess RNA Integrity
steps.instruction: Analyze RNA integrity on an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 using the standard total eukaryotic RNA pico‑chip protocol to obtain the RNA Integrity Number (RIN). Optionally, run a small aliquot on an agarose gel to visualize 18 S and 28 S rRNA bands before the Bioanalyzer. Store the extracted RNA at –80 °C until sequencing. Aliquot the RNA to avoid multiple freeze‑thaw cycles; use each aliquot once. Transport samples on dry ice for quality checks or sequencing.

steps.title: Long‑Term RNA Storage
steps.instruction: Keep the purified RNA at –80 °C until use. Use the RNA as soon as possible for sequencing to minimize degradation.

description: Although numerous methods have been published which describe the extraction of high-quality RNA from pancreas or pancreatic tumors, our method is simple, reliable and reproducible, resulting in extraction of high-quality RNA (mean RIN = 9.0) from mouse pancreatic tumors that is especially well-suited for NGS analyses. Incorporation of these simple tips will help greatly in improving the quality of RNA and make pancreatic-derived RNA more consistently usable for sequencing purposes, saving money and avoiding bias in the sequencing results. With further adaptation, we envision this technique being applicable to the isolation of high-quality RNA from human pancreatic normal and tumor specimens as well.
